title: Jephthah: The Outcast Deliverer and His Vow
summary: Jephthah, driven from his family because his mother was a prostitute, is called back by the elders of Gilead to lead them against the Ammonites. He argues Israel's claim to the land in a long message to the Ammonite king, then goes to war with the Spirit of the LORD upon him. Before battle he vows to offer as a burnt offering whatever comes out of his house to meet him, and when he returns victorious his only daughter comes out dancing.
story: Chapter 10 ended with Israel oppressed by the Ammonites east of the Jordan, crying out to the LORD, putting away foreign gods, and the leaders of Gilead asking who would lead the fight. Chapter 11 answers with the most unlikely candidate: a man his own brothers threw out. Jephthah is the next major judge after Gideon and the disastrous kingship of Abimelech, and his story continues the downward slope the book has been tracing. He is capable, shrewd, and genuinely empowered by the Spirit, and he wins. But he bargains with God as he bargained with the elders, and the result is the darkest private tragedy in the book so far. The victory over Ammon and the loss of his daughter are told side by side, and the reader is not allowed to separate them.
historical:
The events take place in Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan settled by Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. To the east lay the Ammonites, whose capital was Rabbah (modern Amman in Jordan). Their dispute with Israel concerned the land between the Arnon River in the south and the Jabbok in the north. Jephthah's message retells the history found in Numbers 20-21 and Deuteronomy 2: Israel asked Edom and Moab for passage, went around them when refused, and took this region not from Ammon or Moab but from Sihon, king of the Amorites, who attacked them. Deuteronomy 2:19 records that Israel was told not to take Ammonite land at all, which supports Jephthah's point.

Jephthah's figure of three hundred years since Israel settled in Heshbon (11:26) is often discussed in debates about the date of the exodus. Those who hold an earlier date, in the fifteenth century BC, see it as supporting evidence; those who favor a thirteenth-century exodus read it as a round number or as the sum of overlapping judgeships in a rhetorical speech. The chapter itself doesn't settle the question. Tob, where Jephthah gathered his band, was a region north or northeast of Gilead; men of Tob appear again as hired soldiers in 2 Samuel 10:6.
cultural:
Inheritance followed the father's legitimate sons, and a son born to a prostitute had no secure claim. Jephthah's brothers use that fact to push him out, and he becomes what the ancient Near East knew well: a displaced man leading a band of other displaced men, living by raiding or by hire. When the elders need a war leader, they first offer him the title of commander (qatsin, a military chief) and only when he presses them do they promise to make him head over all Gilead. The negotiation is sealed before the LORD at Mizpah, a customary place of assembly.

Jephthah's diplomacy uses the language of the time. He speaks of Chemosh as the god who gives the Ammonites their land, answering them in terms they would accept. Chemosh was in fact the god of Moab (the Ammonite god was Milcom), and scholars explain the detail in different ways: the disputed territory had once been Moabite, Ammon may have been speaking for Moabite claims, or the two peoples' religion overlapped in the region. Vows, finally, were binding promises to God, often made in crisis and conditional on his help (compare Jacob in Genesis 28:20-22 and Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:11). The law allowed rash vows to be dealt with and never permitted human sacrifice, which it condemns as a practice of the nations (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31).
literary: The chapter is built from three sets of negotiations. Jephthah bargains with the elders (11:4-11), with the Ammonite king (11:12-28), and with God (11:29-31). The first two are conducted with skill, and the third is the one he did not need to make, since the Spirit of the LORD had already come upon him in 11:29. The repeated phrase about giving the Ammonites into his hand ties the three together. The narrator is notably restrained after the vow: he reports the daughter's words, the two months in the mountains, and the yearly lament, and says only that Jephthah “did to her as he had vowed” (11:39) without describing the act. The daughter is never named, which makes the yearly mourning of the young women of Israel the only memorial she receives.

outline.t: Jephthah, a son of Gilead, driven out by his brothers
The elders of Gilead bring him back as commander and head
Jephthah's message to the Ammonite king about the land
The Spirit comes upon him, the vow, and victory over Ammon
His daughter meets him, and the vow is kept

doctrines.note: Jephthah's message rests on the claim that the LORD, the Judge, gives and takes land among nations. The victory confirms that the outcome is in God's hands, not the elders' or the Ammonite king's.
The Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah for the battle before he makes his vow. The Spirit's empowering for a task does not make a leader wise or guarantee that his other choices are right.

The vow treats God as someone to be bargained with, as the elders treated Jephthah. The rest of Scripture forbids human sacrifice and presents God as the one who provides, not the one who must be paid off.

words.note: Neder, vow, with the related verb nadar in 11:30 and 11:39. A vow was a solemn promise to God, usually conditional, and Israel took vows seriously (Deuteronomy 23:21-23). Leviticus 27, however, lays out ways people and things vowed to God could be redeemed with money, and the law never allows a vow to require what God forbids. The tragedy of the chapter turns on a vow that should never have been made.

Shaphat, to judge. In 11:27 Jephthah appeals to the LORD as the Judge who will decide between Israel and Ammon. The book is named for this verb, which covers both deciding disputes and delivering people from oppressors. Here the true Judge is God, and human judges are his instruments.

Qatsin, commander or chief. The elders first offer Jephthah this limited military office (11:6), and he negotiates for more. By 11:11 the people make him both head and commander. The shift shows how Jephthah secured power by bargaining, a pattern he then repeats with God.

Olah, burnt offering, a sacrifice wholly consumed on the altar. Jephthah's promise in 11:31 uses the ordinary word for a sacrifice given entirely to God. Its presence is the main reason most interpreters believe he intended, and carried out, a literal sacrifice.

christ: The link to Christ here is thematic, not predictive. Jephthah is the rejected son whom his own brothers drove out and later had to call back in their distress, a pattern seen also in Joseph and applied in the New Testament to Jesus, the stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22, cited in Mark 12:10 and Acts 4:11). The contrast matters more than the likeness. Jephthah thought he had to offer something precious to secure God's help, and his only child paid for it. The Bible's story moves the other way: at Mount Moriah God stopped Abraham's hand and provided a ram in Isaac's place (Genesis 22), and in the gospel God gives his own Son freely rather than demanding a child from us. Hebrews 11:32 names Jephthah among those who acted by faith, which shows that God worked through him despite the vow, not that the vow was right.

hard.q: Did Jephthah really sacrifice his daughter, and why doesn't the text condemn him?
hard.a:
Most interpreters, ancient Jewish and Christian and modern, read the chapter as describing a real human sacrifice. The vow uses the word for a burnt offering, and 11:39 says he did to her as he had vowed. On this reading the narrator's restraint is not approval: Judges regularly reports terrible acts without comment and lets the law, which condemns child sacrifice as an abomination, supply the verdict. The chapter's placement in a book about Israel's moral collapse, and the fact that the daughter is mourned yearly, point to tragedy rather than faithfulness.

A minority view, held by some medieval Jewish interpreters and some Christian readers since, argues that Jephthah dedicated his daughter to lifelong service at the sanctuary, unmarried. They point to her mourning her virginity rather than her death, to the note that she had never known a man, and to the connecting word in 11:31, which can be read as or. Critics answer that nothing else in the Old Testament describes such a vow of lifelong celibacy for women and that the plain sense of burnt offering is hard to avoid. Either way, the chapter does not hold Jephthah up as an example to follow.

questions: Jephthah was rejected by those closest to him and later needed by them. How does the way people treated him shape the way he bargains with the elders and with God?
The Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah before he made his vow. Where are you tempted to make deals with God instead of trusting what he has already given?
The young women of Israel remembered Jephthah's daughter every year. Why might Scripture preserve the memory of someone who suffered for another's foolish promise?
